# Four Positions on Open-Source AI Regulation

---

## 1. Completely Open

**The Case:**
Open-source development has historically produced more secure, robust, and innovative technology than closed development. The Linux kernel, Bitcoin, and modern cryptography all benefited from mass scrutiny. With AI, restricting access prevents the broader research community from auditing for biases, finding vulnerabilities, and improving safety. Additionally, restrictions concentrate power in the hands of large corporations or governments—precisely the actors most likely to misuse AI. If powerful AI is coming, democratizing it prevents any single entity from controlling its trajectory.

**Strongest Counter:**
The "safety through openness" argument assumes that threats will be obvious and that helpful actors will outnumber harmful ones. Unlike code in a Linux kernel, a language model can cause harm *while functioning as designed*—through persuasion, synthesis of dangerous information, or automation of malicious activity. Dual-use risks are asymmetric: a vulnerability in security software can be patched; a model released to millions cannot be recalled. Mass scrutiny cannot catch misuse that requires only a single actor.

**Historical Analogy:**
The early internet and the relaxation of cryptography export controls in the 1990s. Initial restrictions on strong encryption (classified as a munition under ITAR) ultimately failed, drove development overseas, and were abandoned. Post-restriction, the open development of cryptographic standards produced more secure systems through public scrutiny than closed government efforts had achieved. Critics note this analogy has limits: cryptography primarily enables *defense*; language models can actively *offend*.
